excerpt: Angle names trip up more Class 6 students than the maths itself. Here is the NCERT Lines and Angles chapter made plain — every angle type and every angle pair — with two worked case studies and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Class 6 student a protractor and ask them to measure a 40° angle, and most manage it fine. Ask them whether that angle is acute, and half of them freeze. That is the honest truth about class 6 maths lines and angles — the geometry is gentle, but the vocabulary is where marks quietly leak away. This chapter is really two skills stacked together: naming an angle by its size, and spotting how two angles relate to each other. Get both, and the unknown-angle questions that fill the exam paper become almost automatic.

I will walk through the NCERT ideas the way I teach them to a nervous eleven-year-old, then solve two short real-life case studies of exactly the kind the chapter loves to set.

Naming an angle by its size

Every angle in the chapter fits into one of these boxes, sorted by how open it is. The full turn is 360°, and everything else is a slice of that.

Angle typeSizeEveryday example
AcuteMore than 0°, less than 90°A slightly open pair of scissors
RightExactly 90°The corner of a notebook
ObtuseMore than 90°, less than 180°A reclining chair back
StraightExactly 180°A flat, opened book
ReflexMore than 180°, less than 360°The larger side of a clock’s hands at 8 o’clock
CompleteExactly 360°One full spin

The one that trips students is the reflex angle. When two rays meet they actually make two angles — the small one and the big one going the other way round — and the reflex angle is that bigger one. If someone gives you a 70° angle, its reflex partner is 360° − 70° = 290°. Worth drilling, because examiners like it.

Angle pairs: the heart of the chapter

Once a single angle has a name, the chapter asks how two angles sit together. There are five relationships to know cold, and every unknown-angle sum is built from them.

Complementary and supplementary

  • Complementary angles add up to 90°. So the complement of 35° is 55°.
  • Supplementary angles add up to 180°. So the supplement of 110° is 70°.

The mix-up is constant, so here is the memory hook I give every batch: C comes before S in the alphabet, and 90 comes before 180. Complementary is the smaller total. It sticks.

Adjacent angles and the linear pair

Adjacent angles share a common vertex and a common arm, and they sit on opposite sides of that shared arm without overlapping. Think of two slices of the same pizza next to each other. A linear pair is a special adjacent pair whose outer arms form a straight line — so the two angles must add to 180°. Every linear pair is supplementary, but not every supplementary pair is a linear pair (they might be nowhere near each other).

Vertically opposite angles

When two straight lines cross, they make four angles. The two that sit directly across the intersection from each other — not next to each other — are vertically opposite, and they are always equal. This single fact solves a huge share of the chapter’s problems. If one angle at a crossroads is 65°, the one straight across is also 65°, and each of the other two is 180° − 65° = 115°.

Finding an unknown angle

Nearly every ‘find x’ question is one of these relationships in disguise. The method is always the same: name the relationship, write the equation, solve. Suppose two angles are supplementary and one is 3 times the other. Call the smaller one x. Then x + 3x = 180°, so 4x = 180°, giving x = 45° and the larger 135°. No protractor needed — just the rule and a bit of algebra the class already knows.

Case study 1: The park bench signboard

Read the passage, then solve. A carpenter fixes a straight signboard flat along the top edge of a park wall. A wooden support meets the underside of the signboard, splitting the straight edge into two angles. The angle on the left measures 115°.

  • What kind of angle pair do the two angles form? Their outer arms lie along one straight edge, so they are a linear pair — and therefore supplementary.
  • Find the right-hand angle. 180° − 115° = 65°.
  • Name the 65° angle by size. It is between 0° and 90°, so it is acute.

Case study 2: The crossroads near the school

Two straight roads cut across each other outside a school, making four angles at the junction. A traffic sign sits in one corner where the angle is 50°.

  • The angle directly opposite the sign? Vertically opposite angles are equal, so it is also 50°.
  • Each of the other two angles? They form a linear pair with the 50° angle, so each is 180° − 50° = 130°.
  • Is 130° acute, right or obtuse? It is more than 90° and less than 180°, so obtuse.

Notice how one measured angle unlocked all four. That is the whole point of the angle-pair rules — measure once, reason for the rest.

Try the quiz, then the case-study practice

The eight questions below cover every idea from this chapter — angle types, complementary and supplementary pairs, linear pairs and vertically opposite angles. quiz.title: Class 6 Lines and Angles Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on angle types and angle pairs from the NCERT Lines and Angles chapter. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 6 lines and angles: types and angle pairs

questions.q: An angle measures 47°. What type is it?
questions.explanation: It is more than 0° and less than 90°, so it is acute.

questions.q: What is the complement of a 62° angle?
What is the supplement of a 105° angle?
Two angles form a linear pair. One is 130°. Find the other.
questions.explanation: A linear pair is supplementary, so the other is 180° − 130° = 50°.

questions.q: Two straight lines cross. One angle is 72°. What is the angle vertically opposite it?
questions.explanation: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so it is also 72°.

questions.q: Which of these is an obtuse angle?
questions.explanation: An obtuse angle is more than 90° and less than 180°, so 135° qualifies.

questions.q: What is the reflex angle that pairs with an 80° angle?
Two supplementary angles are equal. What is each one?
questions.explanation: If x + x = 180°, then 2x = 180°, so each angle is 90°.

faq.q: What is the difference between complementary and supplementary angles?
faq.a: Complementary angles add up to 90°; supplementary angles add up to 180°. A quick memory hook: C comes before S in the alphabet, just as 90 comes before 180, so complementary is the smaller total.

Yes. A linear pair sits on a straight line, and a straight angle is 180°, so the two angles must add to 180°. But the reverse is not true — two supplementary angles need not be next to each other, so they are not always a linear pair.

faq.q: Why are vertically opposite angles always equal?
faq.a: When two lines cross, each pair of opposite angles is supplementary to the same neighbouring angle. Since both are 180° minus that shared angle, they must be equal to each other.

faq.q: How do I find an unknown angle in this chapter?
faq.a: Name the relationship first — complementary, supplementary, linear pair or vertically opposite — then write it as an equation and solve. For example, supplementary angles in the ratio 1:3 give x + 3x = 180°, so x = 45°.
